knowledgePattern: Count repeated and shared roots of a linear-times-quadratic equation

hints.title: Separate the possible overlaps
hints.body: List the roots supplied by the linear factor and consider how roots from the quadratic might coincide with each other or with that root.
hints.recap: A zero product allows either factor to be zero; shared roots count only once.
hints.pitfall: A repeated root is not an extra distinct root.
hints.pause: Identify the possible ways the factors can supply exactly two distinct roots.

recall.reminder: A zero product allows either factor to be zero; shared roots count only once.

hints.title: Test each mechanism
hints.body: Use the discriminant for a repeated quadratic root; separately substitute the linear-factor root into the quadratic to test overlap.
hints.recap: The discriminant detects repeated quadratic roots, but the full polynomial still needs checking.
hints.pitfall: A candidate parameter might collapse all factors to the same root.
hints.pause: Solve both parameter conditions and verify the complete factorisation for each candidate.

recall.reminder: The discriminant detects repeated quadratic roots, but the full polynomial still needs checking.

solution:
1. The linear factor always gives x=p. To obtain exactly two distinct roots, either the quadratic has a repeated root different from p, or it has two distinct roots and one is p.

2. A repeated quadratic root requires p2−4p=0, so p=0 or p=4. At 0, the full equation is x3=0 and has only one root. At 4, it is (x−4)(x+2)2=0, giving two.

3. For a shared root, substitute x=p into the quadratic: 2p2+p=0. This gives p=0 or p=−1/2. The first fails as above; at the second, the quadratic roots are −1/2 and 1, both real and distinct.

4. The required product is 4(−1/2)=−2. Answer B.
